hints: Look at what fills the gap between the two sugar-phosphate backbones. What type of bases pair together to bridge that space?

Remember the size difference: purines (A and G) have two rings and are large, pyrimidines (T and C) have one ring and are small. What happens to total width if you always pair one large with one small?
walkthrough:
**Picture the DNA ladder**

Think of the two sugar-phosphate chains as the two sides of a ladder. The distance apart stays constant, so each rung of the ladder must be the same length.

The rungs are made of paired bases, so base pairing must control the width.

**Compare purines and pyrimidines**

Purines, adenine and guanine, are big with a double ring. Pyrimidines, thymine and cytosine, are small with a single ring.

A big base paired with a small base always gives the same total width: large + small.

**Apply the pairing rule**

In DNA, A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. That is always purine to pyrimidine.

Because every pair is one large plus one small, every rung is the same length, so the backbones stay a constant distance apart.

options.A: Not true. A-T are held by 2 hydrogen bonds and C-G by 3. Hydrogen bond number affects strength, not the constant width.
options.B: Not true. Nucleotides are not all the same size because their bases differ, purines are larger than pyrimidines.
options.C: Correct. Every base pair is one large purine plus one small pyrimidine, so each pair spans the same distance and keeps the backbones evenly spaced.
options.D: Not true. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases, not sulfur bridges, which are found in some proteins.
